chapter_theme: Civakan finds his mother Vijayai in the hermitage: she weeps and nurses him in her embrace, both take the family's ruin on themselves, and she yields her motherhood to Sunandai and Kandukkatan and claims Nandattan as her own; after six days she teaches him kingcraft (marriage alliances, just wealth, spies, divide and rule, wealth that buys army and land), measures their exile against it, and when Civakan and his friends answer with lion-like confidence in force, she answers with the crow that killed the owls and the lion caught in a net, and sends him to his maternal uncle.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, raised by Kandukkatan
Saccandan's widowed queen and Civakan's mother, living as an ascetic in the hermitage
Civakan's younger (foster) brother, Sunandai's son, called நந்தன் here
Civakan's companions, called குமரர் and மைந்தர் here
Civakan's friend, one of the companions

1911.reading: The moment she sees the boy who has fallen at her holy feet, the mother's eyes fill with tears and sweet milk spills from her breasts over his chest, and crying 'come, my elephant' she draws him into her arms.
1911.event: Civakan falls at Vijayai's feet; she weeps, her milk flows, and she embraces him.
1911.nuance: The milk that flows on sight of a grown son is the epic's sign of recognised motherhood; it answers the burning-ground birth, where she could not nurse him and gave him up.

1912.reading: Forgetting in her love that he is now a grown youth, the woman like a goddess to be worshipped clasps her son tight to her breast and says that her arms' long ache is over, she who had thought her former penance had borne no fruit.
1912.event: Vijayai holds Civakan to her breast like a child and speaks of her grief ended.
1912.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 (தாளையா ... றோளையாத் தீர்ந்த) are hard to divide; the sense that her penance had seemed fruitless and that her arms' longing is now ended is a reading, not a certainty.

1913.reading: She calls herself the base woman who left the king in the sword-fight and left him in the burning forest, and marvels that Civakan Saami, with a chest like the young sun, has come to see her on lotus feet that may be hurt.
1913.event: Vijayai reproaches herself for abandoning husband and child and greets Civakan.
1913.nuance: கயத்தியேன் is strong self-blame: the story told her flight as the king's command and the child's leaving as forced, but the mother judges herself by the result, not the necessity.

1914.reading: Civakan answers that he was born only to see an unperishing victory perish, while his lady mother lived in misery and her well-wishers grieved; he is the baleful tree of the proverb, and she should not sink in the sea of sorrow he has caused, but put away this care.
1914.event: Civakan blames his own birth for the family's ruin and asks his mother to cast off her grief.
1914.nuance: Mother and son each take the blame on themselves in successive verses. The figure in line 3 (விடைமகன் கொன்ற இன்னா மரத்தினேன், a tree of ill that killed a herdsman?) turns on a doubtful word and a story not told here.

1915.reading: With eyes like a deer's and words sweet as honey from a mountain hive, Vijayai says, to gladden her son, that she is not his mother: his mother is Sunandai, always, and his father is not the king but Kandukkatan, great in virtue.
1915.event: Vijayai tells Civakan that his foster parents, Sunandai and Kandukkatan, are his true mother and father.
1915.nuance: The birth mother and queen gives up both her own claim and the dead king's to the merchant couple who reared him; the verse says she says it so that her son may rejoice, which makes it a gift of gratitude rather than a denial.

1916.reading: She goes on that her life's own son is Nandan, not he, and calling 'come here, handsome prince' draws Nandattan to her side, sets his garland and flowered hair right, and gives the bull among his foes a feast of tender love.
1916.event: Vijayai claims Nandattan as her own son, draws him close and tends him.
1916.nuance: The exchange is symmetrical: having given Civakan to his foster mother, she takes the foster mother's own son as hers, so that the two brothers are each other's mother's child.

1917.reading: As a peahen sits gathering her chicks under her wings, the queen holds her sons with both arms, gives each of the youths in turn fitting words of welcome, and feeds them six-flavoured nectar until six days have passed.
1917.event: Vijayai embraces her sons, welcomes Civakan's companions and feeds them for six days.

1918.reading: In a flowering grove of maravam, nagam, fragrant champak, kuravam, kongam and vazhai, sitting apart, the lady speaks on the matter she has weighed, as the next verses give it.
1918.event: After six days Vijayai sits apart with Civakan in a grove and begins her counsel.
1918.nuance: The ascetic mother, in a hermitage grove, gives not a sermon but a lesson in kingcraft; the setting and the matter pull against each other.

1919.reading: She says it is the custom of kings whose rule stands firm to take as wives the daughters of the chiefs who live by the hills and forests, and the daughters of the mighty of the earth.

claims.claim: a king secures his rule by marrying the daughters of hill chiefs and of powerful rulers

1919.nuance: The verse ends in a doubtful word (நோபவே); the sense 'they hold this to be kings' custom' is taken from the run of the counsel. It forecasts Civakan's many marriages as policy as well as love.

1920.reading: She lists what is approved: gathering treasure by justice and right, fixing which is the first and gravest enemy, using a thorn to find out the thorn of enmity, and splitting foes by sowing bewilderment among them.

claims.claim: a ruler should gather wealth only by just and righteous means
enemies are to be found out by setting enemy against enemy and broken by sowing confusion among them

1920.nuance: Just acquisition and divide-and-rule stand in one breath; the verse sees no conflict between அறம் in getting wealth and stratagem in breaking enemies.

1921.reading: Testing spies by other spies, taking learned men as one's eyes, and enlarging the circle of kin around one: these, they say, are the marks of victory for a king who means to win.

claims.claim: a king must check what one spy reports through another
a king should take learned men as his eyes and widen his kin

1922.reading: Wealth, she tells the son on whose chest fortune sleeps, makes victory, makes eminence, makes the diminished into mountains, and makes beauty along with learning.

claims.claim: wealth raises those who have fallen low and brings victory and standing

1922.nuance: பொன்றுஞ் சாகத்தினாய் is best divided பொன் துஞ்சு ஆகத்தினாய், an address to Civakan; the 'diminished' of line 2 are, as 1924 makes plain, the speaker and her son.

1923.reading: From gold comes a fighting army, from that army the land, from the land in turn great wealth, and when that wealth is gathered there is nothing that does not come.

claims.claim: wealth buys an army, the army wins land, and land yields more wealth, so that wealth gathered commands everything

1924.reading: She sets out their state: driven from their land, worn down in treasure, fallen from the standing of their line, and with no learned counsellors here, and asks the young bull what he has resolved; and the generous one replies.
1924.event: Vijayai lists their losses and asks Civakan what he has decided; he begins to answer.
1924.nuance: Each item answers a maxim just given: no land for the army-and-land chain of 1923, no treasure for 1922, no learned eyes for 1921. The counsel was a measure of what they lack.

1925.reading: Civakan answers that when a thunder-voiced lion with strength like fire fights a jackal, what need is there of strategy and good allies; she should not grieve, for the enemy is a snake and Nandan of the honeyed garland and warrior's anklet is Garuda.
1925.event: Civakan dismisses the need for strategy against Kattiyangaran and names Nandattan as the Garuda to the enemy's snake.

claims.claim: against a weak foe a strong man needs neither strategy nor allies

1925.nuance: The claim is answered at once: 1927 restores the weighing of time and place, and 1928 has the lion that leaps without thought caught in a net. The young hero repeats in brave words the trust in force over counsel that undid his father.

1926.reading: 'Is Nandan a Garuda, then?' she says, and weeping, touches the bright and handsome youth with her hand, gazes at him in love and delight, and asks whether shoulders thick and long as diamond pillars could fail to guard the clamorous earth.
1926.event: Vijayai touches and praises the youth whose shoulders she says will surely guard the earth.
1926.nuance: Whether the youth she touches is Nandattan, just named, or Civakan the காளை of line 4, the Tamil does not settle; கலுழ may also be read of the one touched rather than of her.

1927.reading: For those strong in judgment who weigh place and time, fear no undertaking and plan without folly, is anything too hard? In the wilderness a single crow went among the owls in their own place and, while they lay helpless, took the lives of a thousand crore.

claims.claim: those who weigh place and time and plan without folly can achieve anything, even the weak against the many

1927.nuance: The speaker is not named; the verse answers Civakan's 1925 and reads as the mother's. The crow among the owls is a fable known also from the Sanskrit tale collections; here it puts weakness plus judgment above strength.

1928.reading: Men who do not resolve and carry through what they intend are like women whose waists sag under the weight of their jewels; and the lion of the cave, swelling and roaring and leaping upon its prey, fell into the net of hard-eyed men in the dark forest.

claims.claim: strength that leaps without judgment is caught, as the roaring lion falls into the hunters' net

1928.nuance: The lion is Civakan's own image from 1925, turned against him. Lines 1 and 2 are a hard simile; whether they blame the timid or the rash is not certain.

1929.reading: Padumukan, like the fire at the world's end, says that the foes will sleep on the battlefield, that pressing on by their own strength they will win and gain lordship of the great earth where gold lies stored, that they need no others for the fight, and that the lord has only to command.
1929.event: Padumukan vows that the companions alone will win the kingdom and asks only for orders.

claims.claim: the companions' own strength suffices and no outside allies are needed

1929.nuance: After the mother's case for allies and stratagem, the friend repeats Civakan's confidence; the verse sets the two counsels side by side without deciding here.

1930.reading: The peerless youths roar out together that they who have come to the red feet of this broad-chested lord of fortune hold the enemies to be no more than the dew and darkness that come before the great-rayed sun, and their lady should reckon them so.
1930.event: Civakan's companions shout their loyalty and scorn for the enemy.
1930.nuance: Line 3 (எரியிருந் தயரு நீர்மை) is obscure; the sun-and-dew figure of line 4 carries the sense.

1931.reading: As mullai blooms when the rain-cloud appears and the lotus when the sun's chariot appears, so, she says, his maternal uncle will bloom when Civakan's glory appears; he should go to him and, with his word, destroy the enemy who stands open on the earth.
1931.event: Vijayai sends Civakan to his maternal uncle, to strike the enemy with the uncle's counsel.
1931.nuance: Her last word reinstates what Civakan and his friends set aside: the ally (the uncle) and his counsel (சொல்லினோடே) come before the fight.

links.note: At 310 Vijayai, alone in the burning ground by a hostile city, says she does not know how the child could be raised; at 1913 she names herself the base woman (கயத்தியேன்) who left him there.
links.teaches: The mother who was shown as helpless now judges the same act as her own baseness, so the reunion is weighed down by a guilt the narrator never laid on her.

links.note: At 465 the townspeople say the mother who bore Civakan must have done great penance; at 1912 the mother herself, now an ascetic, speaks of her penance as having seemed fruitless until this meeting.
links.teaches: The crowd's easy inference from a splendid son to a fortunate mother meets the real mother's view from inside the hermitage, where penance felt barren for years.

links.note: At 473 the foster father, more to Civakan than a mother, receives him home; at 1915 the birth mother herself declares Sunandai his mother and Kandukkatan his father.
links.teaches: The foster bond the story showed in action is ratified by the one person entitled to dispute it, turning the merchant's care into a parenthood the queen confers.

links.note: The patikam's 24 says only that Civakan took counsel with his mother (தாயொடு எண்ணி) before entering the city; 1918 to 1931 give that counsel as a full lesson in kingcraft.
links.teaches: The summary's two words turn out to hold the epic's most compact statement of royal policy, placed in the mouth of a widowed ascetic queen.

links.note: The patikam's 9 says Saccandan would not hear counsel (சொல்லாறு கேளான்) and was beaten by a plot (சூழ்ச்சியில் தோற்ற); at 1925 his son asks what need a lion has of strategy (சூழ்ச்சி).
links.teaches: The son's first reply to his mother repeats his father's fatal contempt for counsel, so the lesson of the patikam must be learned again within the family.

links.note: 1925 makes Civakan a thunder-voiced lion who needs no stratagem against a jackal; 1928 has a cave lion, roaring and leaping, fall into the hunters' net.
links.teaches: The counsel defeats the hero with his own image: the lion stays a lion, but the reply shows that strength without judgment is just what a net is made to catch.

links.note: Kural 497 says no ally is needed but fearlessness, provided one thinks everything through and acts by the place; at 1925 Civakan claims no strategy or allies are needed because he is strong.
links.teaches: Civakan keeps the couplet's conclusion and drops its condition, and the mother's next verses restore exactly the weighing of place that the couplet made the price of going alone.

gains.a: Civakan's boast is shown to be a half-quoted rule, which explains why the mother answers with place and time rather than with doubts about his courage
gains.b: the couplet's proviso (எஞ்சாமை எண்ணி இடத்தால் செயின்) is shown to be the part a brave young man leaves out, so it reads as a warning and not a licence

links.note: Kural 481 says the crow beats the owl by day and that kings need the right time; 1927 tells of one crow that went among the owls in their own place and killed a thousand crore.
links.teaches: The couplet's even match, decided by the hour, becomes in the epic one against countless decided by time, place and cunning together, so judgment is shown to multiply strength and not merely to time it.

gains.a: the mother's fable gains the authority of a known royal maxim, so it reads as counsel from the books of kings rather than a nursery tale
gains.b: the couplet's image gains a story in which the crow's advantage is pressed home by stratagem in the enemy's own ground, beyond what daylight alone gives

links.note: Kural 500 has the jackal kill the fearless elephant once its feet sink in the mire; 1928 has the roaring lion caught in the hunters' net in the forest.
links.teaches: Both reverse the strong beast by its setting, but the epic puts the reversal in a mother's answer to a son who has just called himself the lion, so the maxim is aimed at a person and not at kings in general.

gains.a: the epic's lion gains the couplet's structure, in which ground and not courage decides, so the net is read as the place chosen by weaker men
gains.b: the couplet gains a living addressee, a young claimant who must hear that his own strength is what the trap relies on

links.note: Kural 445 says a king walks with his counsellors as his eyes and must choose them with care; 1921 has Vijayai give the same rule, and at 1924 she says there are no learned counsellors here.
links.teaches: The couplet assumes a court to choose counsellors from; the exiled prince has none, so the rule becomes a measure of what he lacks and throws the choice back on his own resolve.

gains.a: Vijayai's lament gains force from the rule it cannot meet, showing why she asks what he himself has resolved
gains.b: the couplet gains its limiting case, a ruler without a court, where the eyes it requires must first be found

links.note: Kural 751 says nothing but wealth makes people of no account into people of account; 1922 says wealth makes the diminished into mountains, and 1924 names the speaker and her son as those diminished in lineage and treasure.
links.teaches: The epic turns the couplet, often read as a dry observation about upstarts, onto a fallen royal house, for whom wealth is the way back to the standing birth once gave.

gains.a: the mother's maxim gains a sharper edge, since the Kural's rule about the lowly is applied to princes who have become lowly
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where wealth restores rather than creates standing, which tests whether its rule is only about the low-born

links.note: Kural 760 says that for those who have made bright wealth the other two aims, virtue and pleasure, come together; 1923 makes gold yield army, army land, land wealth, and wealth everything.
links.teaches: Where the couplet makes wealth the way to virtue and pleasure, the mother's chain loops wealth back into power and more wealth, and only her own first condition in 1920, wealth got by justice, ties it to அறம்.

gains.a: the chain gains a measure: set against the couplet, it shows how far political counsel has narrowed wealth's ends to power
gains.b: the couplet's ஒண்பொருள் gains a contrast case, a cycle of wealth for power whose brightness depends wholly on how it was got

links.note: 1919 counts taking the daughters of hill and forest chiefs as the settled custom of kings whose rule stands; Purananuru 336 shows a king hot for a girl whose father will not give her, and the war that waits on it.
links.teaches: The epic's 'custom' is the king's side of a transaction that the Purananuru shows from the chief's side as a demand refused and a battle coming, so the policy's cost becomes visible.

gains.a: the mother's maxim gains the cost it leaves unsaid: a chief's daughter is not always given, and the alliance may first be a war
gains.b: the Purananuru's refusal gains the ruler's reasoning, marriage as policy for a firm throne, which the poem's anger does not state

source_issues: 1911, 1914, 1915, 1916, 1925 to 1929: stanzas printed in half-lines and joined by the build (text flags).
1912 lines 3-4: 'தாளையா ... றோளையாத் தீர்ந்த' hard to divide; the sense is uncertain.
1914 line 3: 'விடைமகன்' doubtful (இடைமகன்?); the figure of the baleful tree is not fixed.
1915 line 4: 'மகிழ்ச்' appears to be a misprint for மகிழச்.
1919 line 4: 'நோபவே' doubtful; the closing verb is unclear.
1922 line 4: 'பொன்றுஞ் சாகத்தினாய்' read as பொன் துஞ்சு ஆகத்தினாய்.
1930 line 2: 'சோந்த' appears to be a misprint for சேர்ந்த; line 3 obscure.
1931 line 2: 'றோதோன்ற' appears to be a misprint for (வெய்யோன்) தேர் தோன்ற, and 'மலருஞ்செம்மனின்' for மலரும் செம்மல் நின்.
